big_case_rationale: A pleading-standard ruling that will govern the large and growing 401(k)/403(b) fiduciary-breach litigation industry across all circuits; high stakes for plan sponsors and participants, though technical and unlikely to lead general news.

semantic_claims.proposition: The majority will hold that ERISA imprudence claims predicated on fund underperformance are governed by the ordinary context-specific plausibility inquiry of Fifth Third Bancorp v. Dudenhoeffer and Hughes v. Northwestern, and that a "meaningful benchmark" comparator is not a categorical pleading requirement: a sound comparator is one way, not the only way, to raise a plausible inference of a flawed fiduciary process, because 29 U.S.C. §1104(a)(1)(B)'s "like capacity ... like aims" language states the fiduciary's standard of conduct rather than a pleading element, and Twombly/Iqbal supply no fund-comparison rule. The Ninth Circuit's categorical meaningful-benchmark requirement will be disapproved on that ground.

The majority's stated ground will be categorical as to pleading law — a rule for all underperformance-predicated ERISA duty-of-prudence claims, not one confined to Intel's alternative-investment-heavy funds — but modest in operation: it will reject the meaningful-benchmark requirement as a freestanding element while declining to hold this complaint sufficient, remanding for the Ninth Circuit to reassess the allegations holistically under the context-specific standard, and it will expressly preserve that comparator allegations remain highly probative, so a complaint resting on underperformance alone may still fail without a sound basis for comparison.
